title: Jihad vs. McWorld: How Globalism and Tribalism Are Reshaping the World
author: Benjamin R. Barber
target_audience: Students and scholars of political science and international relations
Readers interested in globalization and its cultural effects
General audiences seeking to understand global trends in politics and culture
core_themes: The tension between globalization (McWorld) and tribalism (Jihad)
Erosion of democratic values in the face of global corporate interests and local identity movements
Impact of market capitalism and consumer culture on traditional societies
Rise of parochialism and fundamentalism as a reaction to modernity
Challenges to nation-state sovereignty and participatory democracy
primary_purpose: To analyze and critique the dual and opposing forces reshaping the world: homogenizing consumer globalization (McWorld) and fragmenting, identity-driven tribalism (Jihad), and to warn of their combined threats to democratic institutions.

structure_format.narrative_style: Academic yet accessible; uses essays, critical analysis, and case studies
structure_format.organization: Organized around the contrasting forces of ‘Jihad’ and ‘McWorld,’ with chapters dedicated to each concept, their interactions, and their implications for democracy

key_concepts_lessons: ‘McWorld’ represents the spread of global capitalism, media, and technology, producing cultural homogenization and economic interdependence.
‘Jihad’ signifies the revival of local identities, ethnic conflicts, and fundamentalism, often expressed through violence and resistance to globalization.
Both forces undermine democratic governance—McWorld by elevating markets above citizenship; Jihad by prioritizing exclusion and intolerance.
Neither force alone or together necessarily promotes democracy, leaving a void in political participation and civil society.
Democratic institutions are threatened by both the unchecked power of corporations and the divisiveness of parochial identity politics.
A strong, participatory civil society is necessary to safeguard democracy against the extremes of both Jihad and McWorld.
notable_features: Popularized the metaphors of ‘Jihad’ and ‘McWorld’ for understanding late 20th-century geopolitics
Draws connections between economics, culture, technology, and politics
Engages deeply with the fate of democracy in a rapidly changing world order
cultural_historical_context: Written in the wake of the end of the Cold War and the rise of global capitalism, the book addresses the paradoxical simultaneous movements toward international integration and local fragmentation. It gained renewed relevance post-9/11, as debates intensified over terrorism, cultural identity, and the desired shape of the world order.
reception_impact: Regarded as a seminal work on globalization and its discontents
Widely cited across academia, policymaking, and the media for its prescient analysis
Praised for its accessible metaphors and multidisciplinary approach
Some critics argue its dichotomy oversimplifies complex global trends
comparable_titles: The Lexus and the Olive Tree by Thomas L. Friedman
The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order by Samuel P. Huntington
Globalization and Its Discontents by Joseph E. Stiglitz
